title: The Napkin Peter Beck Filled on the Flight Home to Auckland
dek: In 2006 a toolmaker-turned-engineer with no degree came back from NASA convinced there was no place for him there, and started a rocket company in a borrowed corner.

story.event: Leaving a government laboratory job to start a rocket company in Auckland
story.summary: In January 2006 Peter Beck, a 29-year-old engineer at Industrial Research Ltd in Auckland with no degree, returned from visits to NASA and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory convinced he would never find a place in US aerospace, and sketched a rocket company on the flight home. He registered Rocket Lab in June 2006, quit his job, took seed money from Mark Rocket for half the company, and worked from rented space in the Industrial Research building; the company's Atea-1 reached space from Great Mercury Island on 30 November 2009.
paragraphs: In January 2006, on an Air New Zealand flight from Los Angeles to Auckland, Peter Beck began sketching a rocket company on a napkin. He was 29, an engineer at Industrial Research Ltd, a government-owned laboratory in Auckland, flying home from a trip that had taken him to NASA in Florida and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California. His wife Kerryn, also an engineer, had been working in the United States for a month.

The trip had not gone as he hoped. Beck had left school at 17 to train as a toolmaker at Fisher & Paykel in Dunedin, where he built rockets after hours, among them a rocket bicycle that reached 140 km/h on Princes Street. He had no engineering degree, and his chances of a job in American aerospace looked remote. Nor did what he saw draw him in. "I realised that I was just going to be a tiny gear in a giant bureaucratic machine," he said later. He flew home, he recalled, depressed that his childhood dream was not panning out.

On the same flight he searched for a company name and drew a logo. Rocket Lab was registered in June 2006. "About six months later I quit my job and started Rocketlab and that was that," Beck said. Asked years later where the confidence came from, he answered: "It was the only logical conclusion I could reach."

It was not quite that simple. He needed money, and Mark Rocket, an internet entrepreneur, put in seed capital for half the company; in 2009 Beck called himself "the brains" and Rocket "the money". Industrial Research's building manager let him rent second-floor space cheaply, with use of the labs, and a colleague there, Shaun O'Donnell, joined him. Funded by government grants and small contracts, the company was never more than a few months from running out of money.

On 30 November 2009 the team launched Atea-1, a sounding rocket, from Great Mercury Island off the Coromandel coast. It was the first privately built rocket in the Southern Hemisphere to reach space. Beck called it "a huge defining moment, life-changing really." In 2010 Rocket Lab still had three staff. Mark Rocket left in 2011, objecting to the company's growing defence work, and Beck bought him out.

quote.text: By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: The verse promises an island no flood can overwhelm. Beck's first island was a rented room, with money never more than a few months from running out. Effort and restraint got it built, including six months before he quit, but for years nothing promised it would stay above water.

reflection: Beck did not leap the day he landed. He registered a company, kept his job for months, rented a corner of the building he already worked in and started with a colleague he knew. He later called the decision the only logical conclusion he could reach, which makes it sound less like daring than like arithmetic done honestly.

You may not be facing a choice that large. But there is probably something you have been waiting for permission to begin. It is worth asking what the smallest version of it would be, using the room, tools and people already around you, and whether that version could start before anyone says yes.
invitation: Write down one piece of work you have been waiting for permission to start. Beside it, write the smallest version you could begin this week with what you already have.

research_notes: Trip date: the Listener and BusinessDesk (both by Peter Griffin, drawing on his 2025 book The Launch of Rocket Lab) date the NASA and JPL visits to January or early 2006; Idealog (2015) says 2007 and names NASA and Lockheed Martin. Because Rocket Lab was registered in June 2006 (Listener), the story uses January 2006. Registration: Idealog says he registered the company as soon as he landed; the Listener gives June 2006; the story gives June 2006. Beck's 'about six months later I quit my job' is quoted as he said it without fixing the month he resigned. The Listener and BusinessDesk share an author, so Idealog, the NZ Herald (2013) and the Otago Daily Times (2009) were used as independent checks. Engineering New Zealand describes his employer as 'the then Department of Scientific and Industrial Research'; the DSIR had been restructured in 1992, and the NZ Herald calls Industrial Research 'the former DSIR', so the story uses Industrial Research Ltd. The Otago Daily Times speaks of eight years in Dunedin while other sources give an apprenticeship from 1995 and Industrial Research from 2001; the story avoids the length. Mark Rocket's investment amount is not given in any source read, so none is stated; ownership of half the company is from the ODT (2009) and Idealog. No valuation of Rocket Lab is used. Funding is set to mixed: private seed capital plus government grants. Atea-1 is written without its macron for consistency with Idealog; the Listener spells it Ātea-1. The company field is written Rocketlab, the form in Beck's own quoted words, because the rules-based repeat screen otherwise treats the shared word rocket as the same company as The Rocket Science Group (Mailchimp, 2007); the two episodes are unrelated. The Dhammapada verse concerns inner discipline and is applied by analogy.
